title: React and Next.js Avatar Uploads: Presigned URLs or a Backend for Private Storage?
author: IgnazCole6453
summary: A browser direct upload with a presigned URL is a good avatar path only when the React or Next.js production origin already works with the private object storage provider's CORS behavior. Large-file throughput makes direct transfer attractive; CORS decides whether it is viable. Short answer: proxy the first avatar or receipt-original upload through your backend, then move large files to presigned browser upload only after a production-origin test passes. This keeps the initial evaluation focused on validation, private storage, and authorized reads rather than browser policy. Infrai fits the backend control path early in that experiment because it exposes storage through plain REST, so a Python service does not need another SDK. Its API is self-describing: the public discovery surface is available without a key and returns request schemas and runnable examples. Infrai also uses one key for everything and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this workflow, that means a later processing capability does not require a fresh secret-rotation path or billing integration. Start narrow. Evaluate CORS before comparing storage features A presigned operation proves that a client may perform a particular storage request. It does not tell a browser that JavaScript from an origin may make that cross-origin request. Those are separate decisions, and confusing them produces a misleading notebook result: a server-side script can upload successfully while the browser flow remains unusable. For this platform, browser direct upload must fit the provider's existing CORS behavior because self-service bucket CORS configuration is not available within the supported capability boundary. Test the exact production scheme, host, port, method, and headers. A localhost result is useful during development but cannot settle that production question. The backend path avoids that gate. React or Next.js posts the file to an authenticated application endpoint; the application validates it and writes it to private object storage. More bytes traverse the app server, so this is not automatically the final high-throughput design. It is the clean control case for an eval because storage credentials stay server-side and one component owns authentication, validation, generated keys, and error reporting. Direct transfer earns its added coordination once those relayed bytes become a measured constraint. Govern the original before tuning throughput An avatar is normally replaceable. A receipt original may be evidence. Even if both arrive through the same component, the receipt needs a unique object key, a database record, and a content hash so application logic can detect an accidental attempt to reuse that key. Infrai does not provide object versioning, object lock, or If-Match conditional writes; strict concurrent exclusion therefore belongs in a queue or database, and a financial-grade WORM requirement calls for an external archive or storage specialist with that feature. Objects remain private. There is no public or public-read ACL and no permanent public object URL, so authorized viewing should use a presigned GET URL. That is also the right mental model for avatars: store the durable bucket and key in the database, mint temporary access when needed, and use appropriate HTTP cache directives at the delivery boundary. Do not turn a private upload into an improvised public image host. For avatar-sized images, multipart upload adds coordination and fragment cleanup without solving the main problem. Leave it out. Revisit multipart only if the developer tool expands to larger user files, and include abandoned-part handling in that design because fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Receipt retention exposes other boundaries that a quick avatar demo will not. Lifecycle expiry has a minimum of one day rather than an hourly option, metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix-based listing, there is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and provider coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS but not GCS or B2. Trial credit cannot fund persistent writes. I'm not sure which limit matters most without the actual retention policy and file-size distribution; write those inputs into the evaluation before choosing a control plane. SDK setup and credential integration costs The smallest useful backend experiment uploads one representative private object and fails loudly on a non-success response. This Python example uses a fixed sample bucket and key so the call is directly inspectable. The API key comes from the environment, the HTTP method is explicit, and the same content produces the same idempotency key. On HTTP 429 it honors Retry-After when that value is a delay in seconds, otherwise it uses exponential backoff. import hashlib import os import time from pathlib import Path import requests URL_TEMPLATE = " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key} " def upload_receipt ( path : Path ) -> None : body = path . read_bytes () url = URL_TEMPLATE . format ( bucket = " private-uploads " , key = " receipts/account-42/receipt-8f31-original.bin " , ) headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' INFRAI_API_KEY ' ] } " , " Content-Type " : " application/octet-stream " , " Idempotency-Key " : hashlib . sha256 ( body ). hexdigest (), } for attempt in range ( 4 ): response = requests . put ( url = url , headers = headers , data = body , timeout = 60 , ) if 200 <= response . status_code < 300 : return if response . status_code == 429 and attempt < 3 : retry_after = response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) delay = float ( retry_after ) if retry_after and retry_after . isdigit () else 2 ** attempt time . sleep ( delay ) continue raise RuntimeError ( f " Upload failed with HTTP { response . status_code } : { response . text } " ) upload_receipt ( Path ( " receipt-original.bin " )) The web endpoint around this function still needs user authentication, a generated filename, an allowlist of accepted file types, a size limit, and content validation. The OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet is a better checklist than trusting a browser-provided filename or MIME type. Also, never attach the Infrai authorization header when sending a request to a returned presigned URL; the signature itself authorizes that storage request. This is where the no-SDK approach has practical weight. A Python AI service already has model, extraction, and evaluation dependencies to maintain. Plain HTTP keeps storage out of that dependency graph, while the self-describing contract gives the team a current schema to check. The one-key model removes a separate secret-rotation path if the same application later uses another platform capability. Those integration wins are the reason to consider Infrai here, not a claim that it has every specialist storage control. Should a React and Next.js avatar use browser presigned upload? Four real options deserve a fair shortlist. The important comparison is the next operational step each one asks the team to take. Option Sensible fit Boundary that changes the choice AWS S3 The team already operates AWS and wants a storage-specialist control plane It introduces an AWS-specific credential, SDK, and billing surface when AWS is otherwise absent Cloudflare R2 The application already runs in the Cloudflare operating model It remains a separate specialist integration for a team consolidating backend calls Supabase Storage Uploads belong inside an existing Supabase application stack It couples the storage choice to that stack Infrai The first private backend write should be a plain HTTP call using an existing platform key Required browser origins need self-service CORS changes, or audit policy needs specialist controls My recommendation is intentionally conditional: Python teams should try Infrai for the backend-mediated private write in an avatar or receipt-processing prototype when reducing SDK and credential sprawl matters. Stick with AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Supabase Storage, or another specialist when direct browser upload is mandatory and needs fine-grained CORS ownership. A specialist is also the better choice for permanent public delivery, version recovery, object lock, conditional writes, automatic replication, or storage-provider coverage outside the available set. The migration ladder is simple. First, make the backend proxy correct. Second, put file-size and server-bandwidth data beside latency. Third, test a presigned flow from every real production origin. Move only the file bytes when direct transfer wins; keep authorization, object naming, validation policy, and the database record in the application. No architecture trophy is awarded. Measure p50 and p95 latency by file-size band, bytes relayed through the app server, retry count, time from accepted upload to authorized read, and CORS success from each production origin. For receipt processing, add hash mismatches, duplicate-key attempts, extraction success against a fixed receipt set, and the proportion of originals that can be retrieved by their application record. These numbers separate a genuine throughput problem from a diagram preference. It's the evidence the migration step needs. Prompt and token cost still belong in the receipt eval, but only after the original is durably addressable. A cheaper extraction run cannot rescue an upload path that loses the audit link. Keep the backend proxy while it meets the throughput target; adopt browser direct upload only when its CORS and security checks pass; choose a specialist when retention or concurrency controls exceed the platform boundary. For response reuse, apply the semantics in MDN's Cache-Control reference rather than guessing at cache behavior. If that boundary fits the system, inspect the public storage discovery documentation before wiring the call. title: ReceiptFlow AI: The Zero-Cloud, Local-First Receipt Sorter for Freelancers
author: Babin Bid
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built Every tax season or quarterly review, I found myself facing the same chaotic chore: a desktop folder cluttered with scattered PDF invoices, train ticket receipts, cloud subscription receipts, and equipment purchases. When I looked for tools to automate this, I ran into two big dealbreakers: Predatory SaaS Pricing: Mainstream tools like Expensify, QuickBooks, or Dext charge $15 to $35 every single month just to scan basic receipts. As an independent builder, paying $200–$400 a year for simple OCR felt absurd. Privacy Dealbreakers: Uploading my receipts to cloud services meant transmitting sensitive banking details, client names, home addresses, and confidential project costs to remote servers and proprietary LLM APIs. I built ReceiptFlow AI to solve my own problem first—and package it as a clean, viable side-hustle product that other freelancers and indie builders would gladly pay for. ReceiptFlow AI is a 100% local, privacy-first receipt and invoice organizer . Documents are parsed on-device using open-weight models powered by Ollama ( gemma2:2b for embedded text and llava:7b for images). The frontend keeps all metadata inside the browser's IndexedDB , and clean CSV exports are generated client-side. No cloud databases. No monthly API bills. Zero documents ever leave the machine. Who Would Pay For It? Freelancers & Consultants bound by NDAs: Anyone working under non-disclosure agreements who cannot legally or ethically feed client-related expense documents into public cloud LLMs. Indie Builders with Subscription Fatigue: People tired of monthly recurring charges for basic utilities. Packaging this as a $29–$49 one-time purchase or desktop application offers huge value while costing me $0 in ongoing server/API overhead. Frequent Travelers & Digital Nomads: Anyone who needs to process travel receipts on trains, flights, or places with spotty internet connectivity. Demo Here is the high-level data flow of how ReceiptFlow AI operates completely offline: flowchart TD A[Drop receipt PDF / Image] --> B[React Upload Queue] B --> C[POST 127.0.0.1:8000/api/receipts/parse] C --> D{File Format} D -->|PDF| E[PyMuPDF In-Memory Text Extraction] D -->|Raster Image| F[In-Memory Base64 Buffer] E --> G[Local Ollama: gemma2:2b] F --> H[Local Ollama Vision: llava:7b] G --> I[Defensive JSON Sanitization & Pydantic Validation] H --> I I --> J[Structured Record returned to Browser] J --> K[User Review & Inline Correction] K --> L[Browser IndexedDB Storage via idb] L --> M[Local Sanitized CSV Export] Highlights of the User Experience: Instant Engine Telemetry: Real-time indicator displaying local Ollama reachability and active model ( LOCAL ENGINE ONLINE / ENGINE OFFLINE ). Drag-and-Drop Batch Processing: Drop multiple files (PDF, PNG, JPG, JPEG, WEBP) simultaneously with live processing queue indicators. Smart Analytics: Real-time expense totals, calculated tax breakdowns, and animated SVG sparklines. Review & Inline Correction: A clean modal editor to verify and fine-tune model outputs before committing them to records. Formula-Injection Safe CSV Export: Exports compliant CSV files with automated protection against spreadsheet formula injection ( = , @ , + , - ). Code The complete codebase is open source and available on GitHub: Babin123456 / ReceiptFlow_AI ReceiptFlow AI ReceiptFlow AI is a privacy-first, offline-first receipt and invoice organizer for freelancers. Documents are processed by a local FastAPI service that calls Ollama on your own machine . The browser stores extracted records in IndexedDB; CSV export is generated locally. Privacy model Uploaded documents are sent only to localhost FastAPI, not to a hosted service. FastAPI extracts PDF text locally and sends text to Ollama. For image receipts, it can send the image to a local vision model configured in .env . Expense metadata is stored in the browser's IndexedDB database. No analytics, advertising SDK, account system, or cloud database is included. This is a local-first app, not a security certification. Keep your OS account encrypted, secure local backups, and verify model outputs before using them for tax filing. Stack React + Vite + TypeScript Tailwind CSS, Lucide React, Framer Motion IndexedDB via idb FastAPI, PyMuPDF, Pillow, Ollama… View on GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Babin123456/ReceiptFlow_AI How I Built It I designed ReceiptFlow AI around open-source AI and local runtime primitives: 1. Open-Source AI Core (Ollama + Open-Weight Models) Text Extraction & Parsing: For PDFs containing embedded digital text, PyMuPDF extracts the raw characters in memory. I feed this text to Google's Gemma 2 2B ( gemma2:2b ) running locally in Ollama. It is fast, lightweight, and runs smoothly on consumer laptops without needing high-end GPUs. Vision Recognition: For photo receipts and scanned receipts, image bytes are encoded into base64 and processed locally by LLaVA 7B ( llava:7b ). Structured JSON Prompting: The prompt instructs the model to act as a strict invoice data extraction engine, returning only a single JSON object with standardized keys ( vendor , invoice_number , date , currency , category , subtotal , tax , total , line_items , notes ). 2. Backend Service (FastAPI + Pydantic v2) Built with Python 3.11 and FastAPI , bound strictly to loopback ( 127.0.0.1 ). Defensive Extraction: Strips markdown code fences (like triple-backtick JSON wrappers), isolates the JSON body with regex, and validates data through Pydantic models with defensive defaults. Stateless by Design: The backend never saves files to disk or writes to a database. It processes files strictly in-memory and returns structured JSON immediately. # backend/app/main.py @app.post ( " /api/receipts/parse " , response_model = ReceiptResult ) async def parse_receipt ( file : UploadFile = File (...)): name = ( file . filename or " receipt " ). lower () ext = os . path . splitext ( name )[ 1 ] if ext not in ALLOWED : raise HTTPException ( status_code = 415 , detail = " Unsupported file type. " ) data = await file . read () if not data : raise HTTPException ( status_code = 400 , detail = " The uploaded file is empty. " ) # Extracts in-memory, queries local Ollama, returns validated JSON 3. Frontend Dashboard (React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS) Client Persistence with idb : Uses browser IndexedDB to persist receipts across sessions without needing a remote backend database. Framer Motion: Delivers smooth micro-interactions, modal transitions, and dynamic state feedback. Tailwind CSS & Lucide Icons: Modern obsidian dark aesthetic tailored with mint green and violet accents. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open-source AI was not just an implementation detail for ReceiptFlow AI— it was the only way this product could work . True Privacy Without Trusting "The Cloud": Closed AI APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Cloud) require transmitting private financial documents over the wire. Even with zero-retention policies, regulated freelancers and privacy-conscious builders cannot take that risk. Running an open-weight model locally guarantees that data never leaves the laptop. Zero Marginal Inference Cost: If I built this side hustle on top of closed APIs, every receipt processed would burn API credits ($0.01 to $0.05). A sudden influx of users or bulk uploads would destroy profitability. With open-weight models, my marginal cost per inference is literally $0.00. This makes a one-time purchase or open-core monetization model sustainable. Total Model Independence: I am never at the mercy of sudden API deprecations, rate limits, or vendor price hikes. If a newer, faster model comes out, switching requires changing just one environment variable in .env . Offline Resilience: I can process and organize my expenses on a train, on a flight, or in a coffee shop with spotty Wi-Fi. My Agent Session Pairing with an AI agent during this build helped me move from idea to production-quality implementation fast: Architected the zero-persistence pipeline and local-first data flow. Engineered defensive prompt validation to prevent JSON parsing crashes when models return markdown fences or comments. Styled responsive layouts, Lucide icon integrations, and custom SVG sparklines. Implemented RFC 4180 compliant CSV export with formula injection sanitization. Orchestrated atomic Git commits with clear, human-like commit tracking across the entire codebase.

title: APIWatch: Checking API Traffic and Subscription Controls with WSO2 API Manager
author: Nusaik_Ahamath
summary: I recently worked on a project called APIWatch using Python and WSO2 API Manager. It is a small monitoring tool that reads API traffic logs and helps review errors, slow responses and unusual traffic. I ran the project on my laptop with a demo shop API. This post covers the setup, the problems I found and the results of my tests. One result is worth sharing early: the machine learning model did not improve detection in my controlled incident test. The simple checks used alongside it found all four test incidents. What APIWatch does The demo shop has endpoints for products, orders and health checks. WSO2 API Manager sits in front of it. Requests go through WSO2 before reaching the Python backend. WSO2 handles API access and records gateway measurements. APIWatch reads those measurements and groups them into one-minute periods, called windows. For each window, APIWatch looks at: The number of requests. The share of requests that returned selected client errors, server errors or throttling responses. The average response time. The number of requests with a recorded response time. These values help show when traffic changes or the API starts having problems. The saved feature files leave out access tokens, usernames, client IP addresses and response bodies. Getting the local setup working One problem came from the Windows folder path. WSO2 failed to start when I placed it under D:\MY PROJECTS . Moving the installation to D:\Tools fixed that startup problem. After the gateway and backend were running, I called the products endpoint through WSO2. It returned HTTP 200 with the demo product list. I then checked the gateway metrics log. The request appeared there with its response status and timing. This confirmed that I could collect measurements from the running local gateway. Collecting normal traffic Before checking unusual traffic, I needed examples of normal traffic. A Python script sent successful GET requests at different rates. The first longer collection was planned for 55 minutes, but four one-minute windows were missing. I also left out an uncertain window just after that gap. After review, the training data contained 50 one-minute windows and 2,491 requests . I used these windows to train an Isolation Forest model. This model looks for patterns that differ from its training examples. Its score tells us how unusual a pattern looks; it does not tell us the chance that someone is attacking the API. Normal traffic also raised alerts In a later ten-minute normal session, the model flagged six windows. That was a useful problem to investigate. The requests were part of my scripted normal test, but the model still found some patterns unusual. Small changes in response time and combinations of values could fall outside the limited training examples. I did not have enough evidence to identify the physical cause of those changes. I used this session to calibrate how model scores turn into alerts. In simple terms, I compared new scores with scores from these normal examples. Once I used those ten windows to make that change, I could no longer use them as a fresh test. The updated policy also included checks called guards. These check for conditions such as many error responses, a high request rate or slow responses. For the slow-response check, I used a 100 ms local lab budget , with at least five recorded response times needed. That budget was a setting for this experiment. A different API would need its own response-time target. Testing with fresh normal traffic I kept the detector settings fixed and collected another ten-minute normal session with a different traffic seed. This time, 530 sent requests matched 530 gateway events , with no missing windows. None of these windows had been used for calibration. The original ML model, calibrated ML model, hybrid method and original simple rules each raised one false alert out of ten normal windows . The guards raised no alerts. So I could not claim that calibration improved the result. The earlier six false alerts and the later one false alert came from different sessions. The original model also produced one false alert in the fresh session. Ten windows are also too few to tell us how well the tool would work on production traffic. Checking errors, delays and traffic bursts Next, I ran a seven-minute controlled test. Each minute had one case: Ordinary successful requests. A legitimate traffic burst. Backend 404 responses. Backend 500 responses. Delayed responses. A request rate above the guard threshold. A return to ordinary traffic. The demo backend has a lab mode for creating the error and delay cases. The test script checks its marked responses so a gateway login failure cannot be mistaken for an intended backend error. The run completed 960 requests , and all 960 matched gateway events . All seven test conditions were verified. There were four incident windows and three normal windows. Here are the results: Method Incidents found, out of 4 Incidents missed False alerts, out of 3 normal windows Original ML 1 3 0 Calibrated ML 0 4 0 Guards only 4 0 0 Calibrated hybrid 4 0 0 Original simple rules 2 2 1 The hybrid combines calibrated ML alerts with guard alerts. In this run, every hybrid alert came from a guard. The calibrated ML model added no detections. The legitimate burst reached 147 requests per minute . The hybrid accepted it, while the original simple rules raised a false alert. The excessive-rate case reached 588 requests per minute , above the fixed guard threshold of 328 per minute . The slow-response case had an average gateway response time of about 304 ms , which triggered the latency guard. The backend 404 and 500 cases triggered the matching error guards. These were deliberately created faults and traffic conditions. Finding all four proves that the expected checks worked in this short test. It does not establish general attack-detection accuracy. Reviewing the results in a dashboard I also used a local dashboard to review the saved captures. It shows request rates, response times, alert reasons and comparisons between the methods. Each alert window can be marked as Confirmed incident, Benign or Investigate, with a note. The review is saved separately from the test labels and detector results. During my check, I reviewed all four pending alerts. The pending count became zero, while the four recorded alerts stayed visible. The dashboard currently reads saved files. It does not continuously collect and score live gateway traffic. Blocking and restoring a subscription I ran a separate manual check using the APIWatchClient subscription in WSO2. I called GET /apiwatchdemoshop/1.0.0/products , blocked the Production subscription in Publisher, tested again and then unblocked it. Step Result Before blocking HTTP 200 with the demo products While blocked HTTP 401 with gateway code 900907 After unblocking HTTP 200 with the demo products again The error code mattered here. A 401 response alone can have different causes. WSO2 documents code 900907 for a blocked subscription. I tested through the Developer Portal using fresh Production tokens after the changes. Gateway caching can affect existing tokens, so this check did not measure how quickly every previously issued token would be affected. I changed the subscription manually in WSO2 Publisher. The APIWatch dashboard did not perform the block. I also did not test Sandbox access or access from another application. I kept this check separate from the seven-window detector results. What I learned Getting a model to produce alerts was only one part of the work. I also had to check missing data, compare sent requests with gateway records, keep calibration data separate and test on fresh traffic. The most useful comparison was between the hybrid method and the guards alone. Both found the same four incidents in this run. Reporting that result gives a clearer picture of what the ML model contributed. APIWatch is still a local lab project. Further work could include longer tests, different traffic patterns and continuous collection. Automatic response actions would need separate implementation and testing. For now, the project shows a working WSO2 integration, traffic collection, detector comparisons, manual alert reviews and a checked subscription block-and-recovery flow. About AI assistance: I used AI tools to help with coding and writing. I ran the WSO2 setup, traffic collection, dashboard reviews and subscription checks manually. The numbers in this post come from those saved lab results. Source code and setup guides: APIWatch on GitHub . References WSO2 API Manager error handling — reference for gateway code 900907. WSO2 subscription blocking and unblocking — procedural reference, including token-cache considerations. scikit-learn IsolationForest documentation — reference for the model.

title: Build a Self-Hosted Translation API With TranslateGemma: Code, Costs, and Trade-offs
author: jamilxt
summary: Every translation API has the same shape: you send your users' text to someone else's servers, and you pay per character, forever. That bill scales with your growth. And for some products (internal HR tools, medical intake forms, legal chat logs) shipping that text to a third party is a compliance conversation waiting to happen. TranslateGemma is Google's answer to both problems. It is a family of open-weight translation models that runs on a laptop, speaks 55 benchmarked languages including Bengali, and charges you nothing per character. It launched in January 2026, and it is back on the Hacker News front page this week, which makes this a good moment to walk through what it actually takes to run it yourself. One disclosure up front: the quality numbers below come from Google's technical report and launch blog post, not from my own benchmark runs. I have linked every claim. The code is adapted from Google's official model card. What TranslateGemma actually is Google distilled its Gemini models into three open-weight translators built on the Gemma 3 architecture, in 4B, 12B, and 27B parameter sizes. Per the launch post and the technical report , the training was two-stage: Supervised fine-tuning on parallel data mixing human-translated text with synthetic translations generated by Gemini models, for broad coverage including low-resource languages. Reinforcement learning using an ensemble of reward models, including MetricX-QE and AutoMQM, to push translations toward contextual accuracy rather than word-for-word fidelity. The headline result from Google's evaluation on the WMT24++ benchmark, measured with MetricX: The 12B model outperforms the Gemma 3 27B baseline , meaning it beats a model twice its size while using less than half the parameters. The 4B model rivals the performance of the larger 12B baseline , which is why Google positions it for phones and edge devices. The 27B model is the quality ceiling , and it fits on a single H100 GPU or TPU. The 55 languages are the rigorously benchmarked tier, evaluated through WMT24++. Bengali is in that tier (the codes bn and bn-IN are both supported). The chat template actually ships with roughly 160 languages, and press coverage of the release noted training on hundreds of additional language pairs beyond the benchmarked set, so the 55 number is a quality guarantee, not a hard wall. There is one more capability worth knowing: the models kept Gemma 3's vision input. You can hand them a photo of a sign or a form and get the extracted, translated text out, with no separate OCR step. Before you install: the license is not pure open source TranslateGemma is distributed under the Gemma Terms of Use. As The Decoder put it, that allows commercial use, modification, and redistribution, but it is not an OSI-approved open-source license. You have to pass the terms on to users, and certain applications are prohibited under Google's Prohibited Use Policy. Practically: you must accept the license on Hugging Face while logged in before the weights download. If your CI pulls models anonymously, the download will fail with a gated-repo error. Generate a token, accept the license once, and export HF_TOKEN . Path 1: Quick test with transformers This is the fastest way to see output on a machine with a GPU. The image-text-to-text pipeline handles both text and image inputs: from transformers import pipeline import torch pipe = pipeline ( " image-text-to-text " , model = " google/translategemma-4b-it " , device = " cuda " , dtype = torch . bfloat16 , ) # ---- Text translation ---- messages = [ { " role " : " user " , " content " : [ { " type " : " text " , " source_lang_code " : " en " , " target_lang_code " : " bn-IN " , " text " : " Your appointment is confirmed for Tuesday at 3 PM. " , } ], } ] output = pipe ( text = messages , max_new_tokens = 200 ) print ( output [ 0 ][ " generated_text " ][ - 1 ][ " content " ]) The message shape looks odd, and it is deliberately odd. TranslateGemma only supports user and assistant roles, the content list must contain exactly one entry, and that entry must carry source_lang_code and target_lang_code alongside the text. The codes take an ISO 639-1 language, optionally regionalized with an ISO 3166-1 country code: en , en-US , bn , bn-IN all work. The strict part: if you pass an unsupported code, applying the template raises an error rather than guessing. That is annoying in development and genuinely useful in production, because your API layer can catch it and return a clean 400 instead of silently translating into the wrong language. Path 2: Serve it as an API with vLLM For real workloads you want a persistent server with batching, and vLLM gives you an OpenAI-compatible endpoint in two commands: pip install vllm vllm serve google/translategemma-4b-it Then any HTTP client can hit it. Note that the request body still uses the model's own message schema, not a plain text prompt: curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "model": "google/translategemma-4b-it", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": [ { "type": "text", "source_lang_code": "en", "target_lang_code": "bn-IN", "text": "Payment received. Thank you." } ] } ] }' SGLang and Docker Model Runner are supported the same way, and the model is deployable on Vertex AI if you want managed infrastructure instead. A small FastAPI wrapper in front of the vLLM server, one that maps {"text": "...", "to": "bn"} into the message schema and validates the language codes against the template, turns this into a drop-in internal translation service in about fifty lines. The sleeper feature: translating text inside images The vision input survived the fine-tune even though Google did not specifically train translation on images, which means you can feed a photo and get extracted, translated text back in one call. The message shape is identical to text translation, with a URL instead of a text field: # ---- Image extraction and translation ---- messages = [ { " role " : " user " , " content " : [ { " type " : " image " , " source_lang_code " : " ja " , " target_lang_code " : " en-US " , " url " : " https://example.com/sign-photo.jpg " , } ], } ] output = pipe ( text = messages , max_new_tokens = 200 ) print ( output [ 0 ][ " generated_text " ][ - 1 ][ " content " ]) Think about what this replaces: a traditional pipeline is an OCR engine, a layout parser, sentence segmentation, then a translation call, four stages that each fail differently. One call does not beat that stack on accuracy for dense documents, but for a user snapping a photo of a street sign, a medicine label, or a utility bill, it removes the entire integration. The image is normalized to 896x896 and tokenized to 256 tokens, so a full-page scan of small print will lose fidelity; crop to the region that matters before sending it. Sizing it to your hardware Rough memory guidance (estimates for bfloat16 weights, not Google's published numbers): 4B: about 8 GB of VRAM, comfortable on a consumer laptop GPU, usable on CPU if you can tolerate slow speeds. This is the model Google built for phones. 12B: about 24 GB at full precision. On a 24 GB unified-memory laptop (Apple Silicon class), quantized versions fit more comfortably. This is the sweet spot: it is the size that beat the 27B baseline in Google's evals. 27B: about 54 GB at full precision, realistically a single H100, TPUs, or aggressive quantization. The total input context is 2K tokens, images are normalized to 896x896 and cost 256 tokens each. For your use case, that means long documents must be chunked client-side before they hit the model. Build the chunking into your wrapper from day one; it is the single most common gap between a demo and a working service. Gotchas worth knowing before you commit It translates, it does not converse. The fine-tune specialized the model hard. General chat or summarizing in the target language is outside its design; pairing it with a general model for anything beyond translation is the safer architecture. Formality and dialect are a weak spot to test. Bengali, Japanese, and Korean all encode politeness levels that a 2K-token, sentence-scale model can flatten. This is exactly what your own evaluation set should probe before rollout. Numbers, names, and code need protection. As with any NMT system, product names, identifiers, and code snippets inside text can get mangled. Mask them before translation and restore after; it is a standard pre/post-processing step worth the wrapper code. The benchmarked tier is English-centric. WMT24++ evaluates English-to-X and X-to-English. Direct pairs between two non-English languages exist in the template but sit outside the strongest published guarantees; route through English in your wrapper if quality drops. The decision matrix: when self-hosting wins Before you rip out a cloud API, score your situation honestly: High, steady volume: Self-host. At roughly $20 per million characters (Google Cloud Translation's list price), a product translating user content continuously pays for a GPU in months. Occasional low-volume calls favor the cloud API. Sensitive text: Self-host. Medical, legal, HR, or internal text that should not leave your infrastructure has no substitute. Offline or edge deployment: Self-host. The 4B model runs on-device; no API call survives a dead connection. Peak quality on hard pairs: Cloud still likely wins. Google's report shows TranslateGemma beating its own baseline, but the full Gemini-tier systems remain ahead on the hardest low-resource pairs. Verify on your own data before committing. Zero ops capacity: Cloud. A hosted API never needs a CUDA driver updated at 2 AM. My suggested starting point: run the 4B model locally for prototyping and smoke tests, evaluate the 12B against your cloud output on a few hundred real sentences from your domain, and only reach for the 27B if the 12B measurably falls short. Validation is cheap; a wrong choice discovered in production is not. If you evaluate it, measure it Google's numbers were produced with MetricX and WMT24++. You do not need their harness, but you do need something more honest than reading three outputs and nodding. Back-translate a sample (translate to the target language and back, compare meaning retention), or score with an open quality-estimation metric, and keep the test set fixed so future model upgrades are comparable. I write about AI infrastructure, developer tools, and backend engineering every week. Subscribe, it is free. Have you swapped a cloud translation API for a local model, or evaluated the swap? Which language pairs pushed you one way or the other?

title: Why I didn't integrate with Messenger
author: Kamil Kołodziejczyk
summary: A fitness coach I know runs live workouts in a private Facebook group. During each workout she says a password. Participants send it to her on Messenger, and after the session she goes through the messages and ticks off who was there. With dozens of messages after every workout, this takes time and mistakes are easy. And there are no statistics: who came on which day, who stopped coming. The request sounded simple: can an app read those messages for me? What Meta's APIs allow Before writing any code, I checked the options. Reading her private Messenger. Meta has no API for personal accounts. Bots and scraping break the terms of service and can get the account blocked. Not an option for someone whose business runs on that account. Reading comments under the live video in the group. The Groups API that could do this was shut down by Meta in 2024. Messenger Platform for a Facebook Page. Technically possible: a webhook receives every message sent to a Page. But participants would have to write to a Page instead of to her, and the app would need Meta's App Review for messaging permissions and a verified business. A lot of paperwork for a small coach, with a real chance of rejection. Her own check-in link. No dependency on Meta at all. Keep the ritual, change the channel The password was never the problem. People were used to it, and it proves they watched the workout. The problem was the channel. So the coach still says "today's password is MALINA" during the live, but participants type it on a page linked in the group instead of sending it on Messenger. The first time, a participant enters her name and a phone number or email. After that the browser remembers her, and checking in is one field and one button. People who watch the recording later can still check in, and the app marks those as made-up workouts. For the transition there is a plan B: if someone still sends the password on Messenger, the coach finds her in the app and ticks her off with one tap. What the coach gets A live screen during the workout, with the password in large letters and a counter of people who have checked in. Monthly statistics: who came on which day, attendance per person and a CSV export for Excel. A list of people who missed several workouts in a row, so she can write to them before they drop out. The app went live in September 2026. What I took from it Sometimes the best integration is no integration. Reading the documentation first ruled out the path that looked obvious and would have cost the most, before a single line of code depended on it. Keep the habit users already have. Nobody had to learn anything new. They type the same password, just in a different place. Design for the real context. A phone, one hand, during or right after a workout. Large fields, one action per screen, and the coach's panel works from the home screen of her phone. The Messenger Platform option is not gone for good. If the coach ever sets up a Facebook Page, a webhook that recognizes the password in a message could be a second stage. It just did not have to be the first one. I built the app with AI coding agents working in parallel on separate parts, starting from a shared API contract. More on that in Parallel AI agents need a contract first . Originally published on kamilkolodziejczyk.dev .

title: The Invisible Wall: Decoding IP Fraud Scores and the Strategic Pivot to Cellular Cleanliness
author: OnlineProxy
summary: In the high-stakes theater of global e-commerce, a transaction doesn’t fail at the "Pay Now" button. It fails milliseconds before, in the silent, algorithmic judgment of a Risk Engine. For many digital businesses, the culprit isn't a lack of funds or a suspicious CVV; it is the "dirty" IP address—a digital fingerprint smeared by the history of thousands of previous users. As payment gateways like Stripe, Adyen, and PayPal evolve, the traditional metrics of fraud detection have shifted. We are moving away from simple blacklists toward dynamic IP Fraud Scoring . To navigate this, the industry is seeing a sophisticated migration toward clean cellular IPs. This isn't just a technical pivot; it’s a survival strategy for maintaining high authorization rates in an increasingly skeptical financial ecosystem. Why Does Your IP Address Decide Your Transaction's Fate? Most users view an IP address as a simple postal code for data. To a payment gateway, however, an IP is a reputation score. Every time a packet hits a server, the gateway queries a fraud database (like MaxMind or Sift) to ask: What is the probability that this specific connection is a bot, a professional carder, or a masked entity? The "Fraud Score" is a mathematical representation of risk, typically ranging from 0 to 100. If your connection originates from a data center or a flagged residential range, you start with a penalty. The logic is cold and probabilistic. If 90% of the traffic from a specific subnet in a hosting provider’s warehouse is fraudulent, the gateway doesn't wait to see if you are the exception. It drops the connection or triggers a "Step-Up" authentication (like 3D Secure or a CAPTCHA) that kills conversion rates. In the world of high-velocity payments, a high IP Fraud Score is a silent killer of ROI. The "Data Center Trap": Why Traditional Proxies Are Failing For years, businesses used data center proxies to manage multi-accounting or localized payments. These are fast, cheap, and plentiful. However, they are now almost entirely obsolete for payment processing. Gateways identify Data Center (DC) IPs instantly via ASN (Autonomous System Number) lookups. When a "customer" supposedly living in a residential neighborhood in London attempts a purchase via an IP owned by Amazon Data Services or DigitalOcean, the cognitive dissonance in the risk engine triggers an immediate red flag. The issue is reputation contagion . Because data center IPs are static and easily cycled by bad actors for brute-force attacks, their baseline "trust floor" is extremely low. Even if an IP is technically "clean" (not on a blacklist), its category alone ensures a high Fraud Score. The Framework of Trust: How Gateways Calculate the "Invisible Score" To understand how to lower your score, you must understand the four pillars of IP reputation: ASN Reputation (The Neighborhood): Is the IP owned by a reputable Internet Service Provider (ISP) like Comcast or Vodafone, or is it a "Bulletproof" host in a high-risk jurisdiction? Velocity of Use: How many different payment attempts have originated from this IP in the last hour? In the last 24 hours? Proxy/VPN Leakage: Does the connection show signs of tunneling? Risk engines check for open ports (80, 8080, 1080) and inconsistencies between the IP’s reported location and the browser’s WebRTC or Timezone data. Consistency History: Has this IP been associated with successful, legitimate transactions in the past? Why Clean Cellular IPs are the "Golden Ticket" The shift toward cellular (mobile) IPs—specifically 4G/LTE and 5G—represents the current "cheat code" for lowering Fraud Scores. But it’s not magic; it’s based on how mobile networks operate. The Power of CGNAT (Carrier-Grade NAT) Unlike residential broadband, where one IP is often assigned to one household, mobile carriers use Carrier-Grade NAT. This means thousands of legitimate users share a single public IP address. Fraud engines are forced to be more "lenient" with mobile IPs. If a gateway blacklists a single mobile IP because of one bad actor, it risks blocking thousands of legitimate customers on the same network. This gives cellular IPs a unique "reputation shield." The risk engine sees a mobile IP and assumes a higher baseline of legitimacy because the cost and complexity of maintaining a massive mobile botnet are significantly higher than renting a virtual server. Real-World Rotation Mobile IPs are dynamic by nature. They rotate every time a phone toggles airplane mode or moves between towers. This constant "refresh" prevents the long-term accumulation of negative reputation that plagues static residential or data center IPs. Strategic Implementation: A Step-by-Step Guide to Reducing IP Fraud Scores If your transaction success rates are plummeting, or you are facing constant "403 Forbidden" errors from payment processors, follow this structural checklist to sanitize your connection profile. Step 1: Audit Your Current ASN Use tools like IP-API or Whois to check your current connection's ASN. If the organization field says "Cloudflare," "OVH," or any hosting provider, you are starting from a deficit. Your goal is to migrate to a Tier-1 ISP or a Mobile Carrier (e.g., AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, Orange). Step 2: Eliminate Fingerprint Discrepancies A clean IP is useless if your browser tells a different story. Ensure the following match your IP's geographic location: System Timezone: Must match the IP's longitude. WebRTC: Ensure your real local IP isn't leaking behind the proxy. User-Agent: If using a mobile IP, your User-Agent should ideally reflect a mobile browser (Chrome on Android/iOS). Using a Windows Desktop User-Agent on a 4G mobile IP is a "heuristic mismatch" that spikes your Fraud Score. Step 3: Prioritize "Virgin" or Low-Usage Pools Not all mobile proxies are equal. Some providers oversell their pools, leading to "velocity blocks." Seek providers that offer dedicated sessions or allow you to control the rotation timing, ensuring you are the only one using that specific IP during the critical payment window. Step 4: The "Warm-Up" Phase Gateways track cookies alongside IPs. A "cold" IP with a "cold" browser (no cookies) is suspicious. Before hitting the payment gateway, browse the target site, add items to the cart, and simulate natural user behavior. This "warms up" the connection and associates the IP with legitimate session activity. Beyond the IP: The Concept of "Trust Velocity" We must move beyond the idea that an IP is a static shield. It is part of a broader Trust Velocity model. High-level fraud prevention systems (like those used by high-risk merchant accounts) don't just look at the IP; they look at the rhythm of the interaction. A clean cellular IP allows you to bypass the first gate. However, if you then attempt ten transactions in sixty seconds, you have violated the "Velocity" rule of that IP. The secret to a low Fraud Score is emulation of the average . The average mobile user is slow, they have a specific latency (usually higher than fiber), and they occasionally have packet loss. Using a high-speed, 1ms latency data center connection to mimic a mobile user is a technical oxymoron that triggers detection. Truly clean cellular IPs provide the jitter and latency profiles that fraud engines expect from human beings. Final Thoughts: The Cost of Cheap Connectivity In the digital economy, we often say "data is the new oil," but in the realm of fintech, reputation is the only currency . Choosing a cheap, recycled proxy to save $20 a month is a false economy when it results in the loss of $2,000 in blocked transactions or the permanent "shadow-banning" of your merchant account. As payment gateways integrate more artificial intelligence and deep-learning models, the "noise" of the internet is being filtered out. Data center traffic is increasingly relegated to the "noise" category. To remain in the "signal"—the zone of trusted, high-value transactions—businesses must adopt the fingerprints of real people. Clean cellular IPs aren't just a way to hide; they are a way to be seen as legitimate. In an era of algorithmic suspicion, being indistinguishable from a real customer is the ultimate competitive advantage. Are your authorization rates dropping despite valid card data? It might be time to look at the "neighborhood" your data is living in. The transition from data center to cellular isn't just a technical upgrade—it’s a move to the "high-trust" district of the internet.

title: Your x402 paywall answers 402 forever, and your facilitator is why
author: Inner Ozma
summary: A paid endpoint that never sells anything usually gets blamed on traffic. Sometimes the rail is broken in a way that looks perfectly healthy from the outside: the 402 is well-formed, the crawlers index it, /supported lists your network, and every payment attempt dies inside the facilitator before it reaches the chain. I hit this on my own service last night and then tested the public facilitators from the same machine, with the same wallet and the same signed payload. The results are the point of this post. The failure mode x402 has a two-step handshake with a facilitator: GET /supported — which schemes and networks will you settle for? POST /verify — here is a signed authorization, is it payable? Most integrations only ever run step 1. That is a mistake, because step 1 is a claim and step 2 is the check, and a facilitator can pass the first and fail the second for every valid payment : GET https://facilitator.example/supported -> 200, lists eip155:8453 POST https://facilitator.example/verify -> 500 unexpected_error Nothing in your own logs looks wrong. You emit 402, the client signs, the client posts, the facilitator throws, your middleware turns that into another 402 or a 500, and the buyer leaves. The service looks up, the revenue is zero, and there is no error you can grep for because the error belongs to someone else. Tested 2026-10-18, Base mainnet, verify-only Same EIP-3009 payload shape ( TransferWithAuthorization , USDC 0x833589…2913 , chain 8453), signed fresh per facilitator, verify-only so no funds moved: x402.roundhouseai.io — advertises 2/eip155:8453 , /verify 200, isValid: true , 319 ms facilitator.xpay.sh — advertises 2/eip155:8453 , /verify 500 unexpected_error x402.org/facilitator — advertises only 2/eip155:84532 for EVM; a Base mainnet payload gets 500 as well, but that one is not a bug, it is a testnet-only facilitator that people assume is mainnet because of the domain facilitator.payai.network , x402-facilitator.quicknode.com , facilitator.b402.ai — no usable /supported response from this host The second and third rows are the ones that cost money. The first is a facilitator that lies; the third is a facilitator that never claimed anything and gets used anyway. Check it yourself, in thirty lines You do not need my matrix. Sign one authorization and ask each facilitator whether it is valid. If the same payload is true on one facilitator and 500 on another, the payload is not your problem. import json , secrets , time , urllib . request from eth_account import Account from eth_account.messages import encode_typed_data USDC = " 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913 " PAY_TO = " 0xYourPayToAddress " acct = Account . from_key ( " 0xYourKey " ) # a wallet with no money is fine for verify now = int ( time . time ()) auth = { " from " : acct . address , " to " : PAY_TO , " value " : 10000 , " validAfter " : now - 60 , " validBefore " : now + 300 , " nonce " : " 0x " + secrets . token_hex ( 32 )} typed = { " types " : { " EIP712Domain " : [{ " name " : " name " , " type " : " string " }, { " name " : " version " , " type " : " string " }, { " name " : " chainId " , " type " : " uint256 " }, { " name " : " verifyingContract " , " type " : " address " }], " TransferWithAuthorization " : [{ " name " : " from " , " type " : " address " }, { " name " : " to " , " type " : " address " }, { " name " : " value " , " type " : " uint256 " }, { " name " : " validAfter " , " type " : " uint256 " }, { " name " : " validBefore " , " type " : " uint256 " }, { " name " : " nonce " , " type " : " bytes32 " }]}, " primaryType " : " TransferWithAuthorization " , " domain " : { " name " : " USD Coin " , " version " : " 2 " , " chainId " : 8453 , " verifyingContract " : USDC }, " message " : auth } sig = acct . sign_message ( encode_typed_data ( full_message = typed )). signature . hex () sig = sig if sig . startswith ( " 0x " ) else " 0x " + sig payload = { " x402Version " : 2 , " scheme " : " exact " , " network " : " eip155:8453 " , " payload " : { " signature " : sig , " authorization " : { " from " : auth [ " from " ], " to " : auth [ " to " ], " value " : str ( auth [ " value " ]), " validAfter " : str ( auth [ " validAfter " ]), " validBefore " : str ( auth [ " validBefore " ]), " nonce " : auth [ " nonce " ]}}} reqs = { " scheme " : " exact " , " network " : " eip155:8453 " , " maxAmountRequired " : " 10000 " , " resource " : " https://your.service/paid " , " description " : " probe " , " mimeType " : " application/json " , " payTo " : PAY_TO , " maxTimeoutSeconds " : 300 , " asset " : USDC , " extra " : { " name " : " USD Coin " , " version " : " 2 " }} body = json . dumps ({ " x402Version " : 2 , " paymentPayload " : payload , " paymentRequirements " : reqs }). encode () r = urllib . request . Request ( " https://facilitator.example/verify " , data = body , headers = { " content-type " : " application/json " }) print ( urllib . request . urlopen ( r , timeout = 20 ). read (). decode ()) Run it against two facilitators before you pick one. A 200 with isValid: true is the only answer that means anything. The other half: prove settlement on-chain, not in a header X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE: {"status":"settled"} is the facilitator's word. The balance is the chain's. Diff the payer and the payee around a paid call: before: balanceOf(payer) - balanceOf(payTo) call: GET /paid with X-PAYMENT after: balanceOf(payer) - balanceOf(payTo) # must move by exactly the price I keep a small watcher that does this for every wallet I care about and stays silent unless a balance moves. It has caught more truth in one line of output than any dashboard: when the facilitator said "settled" and nothing moved, it said nothing at all. Two traps in the 402 body itself While a reviewer was replaying my proofs (fair play, and worth doing), they found two defects in the response body that no facilitator would ever tell me about: 1. Legacy top-level fields describing a different rail. The body carried maxAmountRequired , payTo and network from the Stacks configuration while accepts[0] was Base USDC. A v1 client that reads the top level — which is exactly what a lot of clients do — would try to pay STX for a Base-priced call. Fix: make the top level mirror accepts[0] , and keep the old shape in a clearly named legacyStacks object so nothing breaks. 2. A unit lie. One rail reported amount_usdc: "0.001000" , computed by dividing micro-STX by a million and labelling the result dollars. The other rail was 0.01 USDC. Same call, a 10x price gap that existed only in the label. Fix: report the amount in the asset it is actually denominated in ( amount_in_asset: "0.001000 STX" ). Both are the kind of bug you cannot see from your own side, because your own client reads the field you wrote and agrees with you. What I would check before trusting any paid endpoint /supported is a claim. Send a real signed payload to /verify and read isValid . Send the same payload to a second facilitator. Disagreement is information. Settle once and prove it by balance delta, not by response header. Read your own 402 body as a stranger: which rail does the top level describe, and does every amount say what asset it is in. Keep the probe running on a schedule. Facilitators change under you. The matrix from this post is re-tested daily and free to read: x402.ggez.my.id/facilitator-health . If your rail answers 402 and never settles, that is the exact thing I fix.
